title: The Woman on the Landing
passages:
The causeway stretched ahead, a spine of stone through the grey marsh. Rain had softened the edges of everything. Ákos walked with his notebook pressed against his chest under his coat, the outline of it a second heartbeat. Tomas kept to the left side, his empty sleeve pinned flat, eyes scanning the water where the current pushed against the pilings. They did not speak for the first half-mile. The marsh sounds filled the silence: wind in the reeds, the slap of water on stone, the occasional cry of a bird they could not see.

"He didn't look back," Tomas said finally. His voice was low, pitched to carry only between them. "Kornél. At the smokehouse. He took the name and walked out like he'd collected a debt."

"He didn't collect anything," Ákos said. "The doll gave it to him. The ledger says I'm owed. That means the debt runs the other way."

"Does it?" Tomas glanced at him sideways. "The book says *fragment held by another*. That's not a debt. That's a location. Kornél has the piece. The hut keeper has the price. You have the name written twice and a hollow where Elise used to be."

Ákos's fingers tightened on the notebook through his coat. "I have the name in my book. The ledger didn't take that. Maren said it would, but it hasn't."

"Maren also said the hearthstone going cold means something she won't name. Ilka won't name it either. Two women who know, and neither will speak. That tells me the price is higher than we're guessing."

They rounded the first bend. The river widened here, the current slowing into a sluggish pool. Ahead, the pilot's hut sat on its stilts, smoke curling from its chimney into the flat light. But the door stood open. And on the landing, a figure waited — not Kornél, not the hut keeper. A woman in an oilskin coat, hands tucked into her belt, watching the causeway like she had been expecting them.

The woman did not move as they came up the causeway. Up close she was younger than the coat made her look, forty or so, her face weathered to the color of the reeds. "Ákos Vass," she said. "Tomas. You're late. He's been gone an hour."

"Where?" Tomas said.

"Up. Past the second bend, where the water goes white. I sold him wind." She said it the way Ilka said things, plainly, as if the words cost her nothing. "He paid with the name. The one he came to collect. He had it in his mouth and he gave it back to me for the current."

Ákos felt the notebook against his chest. "Then the fragment—"

"Is here." She drew her hand from her belt. In her palm lay a coil of dark thread, and it was warm; he could feel the heat from where he stood, the way you feel a stove across a room. "He left it. Said the boy would come. Said the patron's name was written and the debt ran the wrong way." Her fingers closed over it. "I don't give it back for nothing. The hut trades in parts. You know that."

"I don't have a part to give."

"You have that." She nodded at his chest, at the shape under the coat. "A book that takes a name and charges nothing. That's a part of you it hasn't eaten yet. I'll take it, and the thread is yours."

Tomas stepped between them. "That book's all he's got of her."

"Then he can carry the thread instead," the woman said, "and lose the name twice."

Ákos looked at the warmth coming off her closed hand. He thought of the cold hearthstone, and the two women who would not say what cold meant. "No," he said. He drew the notebook out and opened it to the last page, where Elise's name sat in his own hand. "I'll write you down first. Then you'll be carrying the debt, not me."

"That's not how the hut works."

"It's how my book works." He wrote her name beneath Elise's — Ruzsa — and the ink went in without a sound, and nothing left him. But the page felt heavier under his fingers, the way a full cup is heavier than an empty one, and he understood that Maren had been right about the price, only wrong about the day.

Ruzsa looked at the book a long moment. Then she opened her hand and the thread was in Ákos's palm, warm as a coal, and her fingers closed on the notebook. "It won't open for you," she said. "It opens for the carrier. He's past the second bend, at the white water. Don't stop there."
